As an aid to future participants as well as question designers, this article describes how to connect legal questions taken from past Japanese bar exams to relevant statutes (articles of the Japanese Civil Code, Task 3) and how to construct a Yes/No question answering system for legal queries (Task 4) incorporating back-ground materials on Japanese law. We restructured the given data to a dataset which contains all possible combinations of queries and articles as continuous strings as our samples. In this way, the difficult pairing task has been turned into a simpler classification task and samples for training became sufficient in num-ber. Next, we used three BERT-based models to solve binary questions in order to achieve stable performance. As a result, the model achieved an F2-score of 0.6587 in Task 3 (ranked 1st) and an accuracy of 0.6161 in Task BV","content-domain":{"domain":[],"crossmark-restriction":false},"abstract":"<jats:p>Legal judgment prediction (LJP) using large language models (LLMs) is increasingly explored; however, its practical deployment remains constrained by hallucinations and limited evidentiary traceability, challenges that are especially acute in under‑resourced, statute‑centric Arabic legal systems. This paper introduces ArabLJP, an evidence‑grounded and retrieval‑augmented framework that reframes Arabic LJP as statute‑conditioned judgment generation rather than label‑only classification. ArabLJP integrates (i) a reasoning-preserving Saudi commercial‑law dataset that explicitly retains factual narratives, judicial reasoning, and operative rulings; (ii) a hybrid "Smart RAG" retrieval pipeline that combines lexical matching, semantic embeddings, and LLM‑guided query refinement and reranking, with priority grounding in statutes explicitly cited in case materials; and (iii) a hallucination‑aware, multi-dimensional evaluation protocol that measures semantic alignment, entity and numeric consistency, and outcome fidelity, with explicit penalties for unsupported factual inventions. The framework is evaluated under controlled experimental conditions across three modeling paradigms: prompt‑only generation; retrieval‑augmented structured prompting; and parameter‑efficient supervised adaptation, and multiple LLM backbones, including gpt‑40‑mini and four open‑weight models (LLaMA‑3.2, Qwen‑3, Phi‑4, and DeepSeek). Empirical results demonstrate that evidence‑grounded retrieval and structured prompting substantially reduce hallucination strength and improve ruling fidelity relative to prompt-only baselines, while supervised adaptation yields further gains in semantic and stylistic alignment with reference judgments. Overall, ArabLJP shows that disciplined statutory grounding, structured judicial prompting, and reliability-oriented evaluation measurably improve LJP robustness in Arabic, statute‑centric legal settings. The framework provides a reproducible methodological baseline for studying and mitigating hallucinations in Arabic LJP, while underscoring that fully reliable automated legal reasoning remains an open research                   <jats:p>
                    The statute book is a large, complex system; a vast corpus of texts dating back to the thirteenth century, now evolving at a rate of around 100,000 words a month
                    <jats:sup>1</jats:sup>
                    . The volume and pace of change combine with the constraints of current generation of digital tools to present a real barrier to researchers, limiting the type of research that is currently possible. The statute book is simply too big, and changes too rapidly, for any one person to easily comprehend. This situation is transformed if you view legislation as data, and then apply big data technologies and new data analysis techniques to that data. The aim of the Big Data for Law research project
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    is to do just that; applying the latest analytical techniques to legislation, making it possible to research, interrogate and understand the statute book as a whole system. An important part of the initiative is to make available the raw data for conducting this type of research, alongside new tools and methods for working with the content. In this article, John Sheridan, Head of Legislation Services at The National Archives, sets out some of the ideas that underpin the project and describes the new service that researchers can use from Spring 2015.
